content: Kawasaki disease is the leading cause of acquired heart disease in children in developed countries. This condition can result in damage to the coronary arteries, which supply blood to the heart. Early diagnosis is critical because timely treatment can prevent these potentially severe cardiac complications. Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) is a widely accepted treatment for Kawasaki disease, aimed at reducing the risk of coronary artery abnormalities (CAAs). The purpose of this review was to assess the effectiveness of IVIG in treating Kawasaki disease and preventing its associated cardiac complications in children. To achieve this, electronic searches were conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Peripheral Vascular Disease Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CINAHL, with the last search performed in March 2003. References from relevant articles were also reviewed, and experts in the field were contacted to identify any unpublished studies. Only randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating IVIG for Kawasaki disease were included in the analysis. The initial search identified 59 trials, but only 16 met the inclusion criteria after thorough evaluation. Data from these trials were extracted and assessed for quality by at least two independent reviewers. The results were combined for meta-analysis using relative risk ratios for categorical data and weighted mean differences for continuous data. A random-effects statistical model was employed to account for variability across studies. The meta-analysis comparing IVIG to placebo demonstrated a significant reduction in the occurrence of new coronary artery abnormalities (CAAs) at 30 days in children treated with IVIG. The relative risk (RR) was 0.74, with a 95% confidence interval (CI) of 0.61 to 0.90, favoring IVIG. However, no statistically significant differences were observed beyond the 30-day mark. A subgroup analysis that excluded children with pre-existing CAAs at the time of enrollment also showed a significant reduction in new CAAs in those receiving IVIG, with an RR of 0.67 (95% CI: 0.46 to 1.00). There was a trend toward benefit at 60 days, although this did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.06). Dose comparisons revealed that higher doses of IVIG were associated with a greater reduction in the incidence of new CAAs. Specifically, a comparison of 400 mg/kg/day for five days versus a single dose of 2 gm/kg showed a statistically significant reduction in CAAs at 30 days, with an RR of 4.47 (95% CI: 1.55 to 12.86) favoring the higher single dose. Additionally, the higher dose was associated with a shorter duration of fever. No significant differences were observed between different IVIG preparations, and there were no statistically significant differences in adverse effects across treatment groups. Based on these findings, the authors concluded that children meeting the diagnostic criteria for Kawasaki disease should be treated with IVIG at a dose of 2 gm/kg administered as a single infusion within 10 days of symptom onset. This approach is effective in reducing the risk of coronary artery complications and improving clinical outcomes.
